title: Bibi Viro
hookLine: Guru Hargobind's daughter, whose wedding went on amid battle

cards: The sweets were already made. The groom's family was on the road. The day had been fixed, and the whole household was counting toward it.

Then word came that soldiers were marching on Amritsar. It's a familiar shape: the celebration planned for months, and then the phone call, the diagnosis, the storm, the bad news that lands the same week.
Do you call it off? Guru Hargobind's household faced that question with swords drawn.

teach.b: Bibi Viro was the daughter of Guru Hargobind. Her wedding had been arranged and the day was set. Then trouble came.

Tradition says it began with a quarrel between Sikhs and a royal hunting party over a hawk, and ended with troops sent against the Guru at Amritsar, just as the wedding drew close. Guru Hargobind had to fight.
But he didn't cancel his daughter's wedding.
Tradition says he sent the women and the bride away from the fighting to a nearby village called Jhabal, and sent word to the groom's family to meet them there. The battle was fought at Amritsar.
And at Jhabal, on the day that had been fixed, Bibi Viro was married. Tradition says the Guru himself came to give his daughter away once the fighting was over.

Picture it: smoke over one town, wedding songs in another not far away, the same family, the same day. The story doesn't pretend the danger wasn't real, and it doesn't pretend the wedding didn't matter.
It holds them together. In Sikh teaching, a householder's life is not a lesser path than a life of withdrawal.
Marriage, children, cooking, celebrating: these are part of the way, not distractions from it. In this story, a wedding isn't given up the moment things get hard.
It's one of the things worth protecting, and protecting it meant a new village, a message on the road to the groom's family, and a father arriving after the battle to give his daughter away.

how: Sikhs remember Bibi Viro's wedding as part of the story of Guru Hargobind's battle at Amritsar, and Sikh weddings, the Anand Karaj, are celebrated as a sacred part of householder life.

games.q: you're Guru Hargobind. troops are marching on Amritsar and your daughter's wedding is days away. what do you do?
o: call off the wedding until the danger passes.
send the bride to a nearby village and keep the date.
hold the wedding in Amritsar anyway.
games.why: tradition says he sent her to Jhabal, fought at Amritsar, and the wedding went on as planned.

practice: Think of one good thing coming up, yours or someone else's, that the hard news around you might crowd out: a birthday, a small anniversary, a friend's good result, a meal you'd planned.
See it clearly, then decide, gently, that it will still happen, maybe smaller, maybe somewhere else, like the wedding moved to Jhabal. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bibi Viro; Bibi is a respectful title for a woman.
